analysis.one_liner: Raises civil fines for companies that repeatedly violate environmental laws or cause catastrophic pollution releases.
analysis.headline: The bill was introduced in July 2000 with no cosponsors and died in the Senate Environment and Public Works Committee without a hearing or a vote.
analysis.plain_summary: The bill would have let the EPA add extra fines when a company violates the same environmental law again at the same site, with the surcharge growing from 25% to 100% of the daily maximum for each repeat offense. It would also set minimum per-release fines tied to the amount of pollution discharged in a catastrophic event, with the highest fines when people are injured and the environment is damaged. It would have given the EPA a new emergency power to order or sue companies that create imminent health or environmental dangers, and to route fines up to $10 million into a fund for cleaning up those threats.
analysis.who_benefits: People who live near facilities that pollute repeatedly or suffer a major release: the higher fines are meant to make repeat violations cost more than they earn, and the emergency authority would let the EPA move faster to stop an ongoing threat to health. Fines collected would also pay federal cleanup costs.

how_it_helps.text: Adds escalating surcharges for repeat violators: 25% extra on the maximum daily fine for a first repeat violation, 50% for a second, and 100% for a third and every one after that.

Sets minimum additional fines for catastrophic releases, scaled to the amount of hazardous air pollutants, criteria air pollutants, ozone-depleting substances, or hazardous substances emitted, with the highest minimums when a release causes both serious injury or death and serious environmental damage.

Lets the EPA issue emergency orders or sue companies creating an imminent and substantial endangerment, with fines of $25,000 to $10 million paid into a Health and Environmental Trust Fund used to pay federal costs of addressing those threats.
Closes a loophole the bill's findings identify: daily penalty maximums under existing law may not be large enough to reflect the real harm of a single catastrophic event.
Prevents companies from dodging the repeat-violator surcharge by transferring a facility to a related party, such as a corporate affiliate or predecessor from a merger.

analysis.who_pays: Companies that pollute repeatedly or cause large releases: chemical plants, refineries, waste handlers, and other regulated facilities would face fines of up to double the existing daily maximums, plus new per-release minimums and possible mandatory preventive measures like extra monitoring and training.
analysis.who_pays_short: Repeat-polluting companies and large industrial facilities

drawbacks.text: The surcharge raises the cost of doing business at noncompliant facilities, and some of that cost would likely be passed on in prices or absorbed in jobs at marginal plants.

The bill counts a release as catastrophic even when it only creates the 'potential' for serious harm, and sets minimum fines per pound or per ton emitted, so a company could owe a very large mandatory fine for a release that in the event caused no actual injury.

The 'repeat violator' definition reaches violations of any environmental law at the same site within three years, so a company could face the top surcharge for violations of different statutes at one facility, which critics could call punishing an umbrella record rather than the specific offense.

analysis.benefit_vs_cost: The design is aimed at a real gap: fines that repeat violators can shrug off and daily maximums too small for one-time disasters. The cost falls on the companies that violate, which is the point of deterrence, but the mandatory per-pound minimums and 'potential harm' trigger could produce penalties out of proportion to actual harm in some cases, and the bill offers no small-business accommodation. On balance a defensible enforcement-strengthening bill whose costs fall mainly on noncompliant companies.

outcome.mechanism: It was introduced and referred to the Senate Environment and Public Works Committee in July 2000, and the committee never took it up before the 106th Congress ended in January 2001.

narrative.text: Sen. Torricelli introduced the bill on July 26, 2000, and it was read twice and referred to the Committee on Environment and Public Works.
No further action — no hearing, markup, or floor vote — appears in the bill's action history before the Congress ended.

outcome.who_came_out_ahead: Companies that violate environmental laws repeatedly kept facing only the existing penalty maximums, with no added deterrence for the communities around them. The public gained nothing because the bill never moved.

for.name: Sen. Robert Torricelli
for.role: U.S. Senator from New Jersey; bill's sole sponsor
for.what_they_did: Introduced the Zero Tolerance for Repeat Polluters Act and made introductory remarks on the Senate floor.

against.name: Senate Committee on Environment and Public Works
against.role: Committee of referral; no chair or member acted on the bill
against.what_they_did: Received the referral on July 26, 2000 and never held a hearing, markup, or vote on it before the Congress ended.

sides.party_line_note: No votes were ever taken and no cosponsors signed on, so there is no record of where either party stood; the only recorded action is a Democratic senator's introduction and a Senate committee's inaction.

industries.industry: Industrial polluters (chemical plants, refineries, waste and water dischargers)
industries.note: The bill would raise their cost of violating environmental laws by up to doubling daily fines for repeat offenses and adding mandatory minimums for catastrophic releases. Those fines exist to stop pollution that harms nearby residents, so the industry's interest in keeping fines low runs against the public's interest in enforcement.
